title: Edward Clem's country band and replacing Bob Lyons
summary: Dawson joined Clem's Pelican band on bass, took Bob Lyons's place, travelled the railroad, and describes Clem and Joe Alva as readers.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: There were a couple of other real old time trumpet players we wanted to ask about. One is Clem, Edward Clem.
Edward Clem, yeah, that I played with him. Now that's a country band. He had more work, more country job than a band in here. He was, he could see that Southern Pacific and TP.

He was out every week. Yeah. He was on that road. Hammond, Ponchatoula, Bugalusa. I've seen the time we'd go to Bugalusa and stay, four nights out there playing. Yeah, Edward Clem. He was a good trumpet player. And he had Willie Warner, was playing clarinet. Old fella called Willie Warner. And Sugar, fella called Sugar. I already know his first name. We always did call him Sugar, you know. Trombone. That was a vowel trombone he had. Didn't have no sliders out. And so we, let's see, let's see how many more we had. I think Frank Adusin played with him a good while. Frank Adusin played and then he got, let's see, he had some old fella they called old C-Net. Old man C-Net on the violin. And I was playing, well they had Bob Lyons was playing bass. Bob Lyons played bass with him a long time and Bob was used to like his T, you know, he'd get a lick at him and he'd blow them up. And he got mad with Bob Lyons. I used to take it, that's how I started most practice learning how to play, carrying Bob's bass all around, you know. I'd carry his bass on the job. So he said, well, you want to play in the band? He said, we're going to let Bob go. I said, no, I wouldn't want to do that. So that time they had caps with their names, you know, Pelican. Pelican of band, you know. So he said, well, you go in, because me and Bob are good friends, you know. They say, you go tell him in the morning to give you that band for the cap, and you can take his bass. He said, if you don't take it, we're going to hire somebody else. He'd rather have you.

Yeah. He said, oh, they didn't want him no more. They got tired of him. So he said, we're going to hire you. We want you on the bass. He said, you can play and shoot us. And he was living up here on Padilla right there by Ramport, upstairs there.
I remember he had a shoeshine place. Yeah, well. At Eagle Saloon.

Oh, that was before that shoeshine place. Before then. Yeah, that was before then. He was living right there. You know where the old Zulu club was on the side? Yeah. In that corner, right near Ramport Street. Yeah. Two-story place there. Well, he was, I went there and he had a room upstairs. You know, he didn't have an apartment, you see. And I told him what Clem said. He said, well, you go ahead. He was kind of an independent fellow, you know. He said, you go ahead and play with him. I said, no, I don't want to do that, Bob. I want to take your job. I wouldn't do that. I said, I'd rather not. I just wanted to let you know so you can go on and see him. Maybe you can iron this thing out with him and get with him and talk. No, I wouldn't want nothing to do with him no more. Well, he's got a hot shot on. He said, he gave me the, the name. Yeah, you go ahead. I don't hold nothing against you. He said, go ahead. I don't. So I went on then. I told him, all right. I accepted. And so I played with him for a long time after that, you know. A little bugger loose, hammering, pauncher too, and all up that road. Well, at that time, you know, we could get on the train and he'd just go to see the conductor and fix it up and we'd go right on and go anywhere we want to see. They didn't charge you. We'd wear, we'd wear, we'd, well, he used to attempt that fare business, you know. We'd leave it up to him. Edward. Edward Clam, yeah. Well, we used to wear uniforms at the time, you know, like the, like the, like the fatigue coach, yeah. And the cap. Yeah.
The braid, the braid down the sides, you know, on the sleeve cuff. Yeah. And the cap, you know, had a check in front, strap in front and then the name on the cap, in front of the cap.
What, what kind of a father was he, what was his appearance? Was he a tall father? Oh, a clam? Yeah.

Well, no, he wasn't so too, he was kind of, a little heavy set. He was just about on the built of Mr. Russell there. About the built of him and he had, he used to wear black glasses on the count of one eye, you see. He had one eye.

Dark glasses? Dark glasses. Never, never seen without them glasses. Hide that, that eye, you see. That one eye put out a long time ago when he was a kid. And he only had one eye. He was just something like Joe Alva. Joe Alva had a cat rack eye and he only had one good eye, Joe Alva had. He only had one that he, but he could see better with that one eye than a whole lot of them Joe could see with both eyes. He could read. I mean sight reader. Yeah. I don't mean to take a piece of music and spell like a whole lot of them do and have to take it a half hour, an hour or so before they could get the sense of it.

He could take a piece of music right out the shop and put it right on up there and say, well alright let's go. Yeah. And take it right from the top on down and read it, sight reader. That's the kind of musician he was, Joe Alva was. Good. One eye. What's that? Clem could read pretty good too. He was a reader? Ed Ball Clem, yeah. He was a reader. But he used most of that sheet music, you know? Piano copies. Yeah. And he know how to arrange, he could take that piano copy and arrange different parts for different men in the band. He was good on that. Well that band there, he was, that Pelican band there had plenty of weight. Anyway. Everything in the country, it kept him going, you know? And I made good money with that band. That's a big deal.
